title: Prime-to-characteristic finite Weil pairings and their transition identities
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $A,B$ be abelian varieties over $k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety], and use their dual varieties, normalized Poincare sheaves and dual pullbacks from [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus]. Let $\ell$ be a prime different from $\operatorname{char}k$. For $n\geq1$ write $A[\ell^n](k)=\{x\in A(k):\ell^nx=0\}$ and $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)=\{z\in k^\times:z^{\ell^n}=1\}$. There are canonical bilinear pairings, written multiplicatively in the target,
$$w_{A,n}:A[\ell^n](k)\times A^\vee[\ell^n](k)\longrightarrow\mu_{\ell^n}(k),$$
namely the finite Weil pairings associated with the normalized Poincare sheaf. They are perfect: evaluation identifies either finite abelian group with the group of homomorphisms from the other into $\mu_{\ell^n}(k)$. For $u\in A[\ell^{n+1}](k)$ and $v\in A^\vee[\ell^{n+1}](k)$,
$$w_{A,n+1}(u,v)^\ell=w_{A,n}(\ell u,\ell v).$$
For every group-scheme homomorphism $a:A\to B$ [def-sc-group-scheme], and $x\in A[\ell^n](k)$, $y\in B^\vee[\ell^n](k)$,
$$w_{B,n}(a x,y)=w_{A,n}(x,a^\vee y).$$
For every invertible sheaf $L$ on $A$ [def-sc-invertible-module], with $\lambda=\phi_L$ as in [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus], and $x,y\in A[\ell^n](k)$,
$$w_{A,n}(x,\lambda y)=w_{A,n}(y,\lambda x)^{-1}.$$
No isogeny or ampleness assumption on $L$ is made.

source.place: Chapter I §13, printed pp.57–58: finite pairing construction and nondegeneracy, Lemma 13.1 (m=ell^n), Proposition 13.2(a),(d), read at finite torsion level (reduction of the integral formulas); also §9 Theorem 9.1 and Cartier-dual description on p.41. Only skew symmetry, not alternation at finite even level, is asserted.

proof.text:
First identify the two duals used below, without assuming their group laws agree. For each abelian variety $C$, [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus] and [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus] represent the same functor of rigidified algebraically trivial families over $\operatorname{Spec}k$. The hypotheses of the latter hold: commutativity is [lem-sc-av-commutative], and the other properties are in the definition of an abelian variety. Yoneda gives an isomorphism $\psi:C^\vee\simeq D$ preserving $0$ and the universal rigidified sheaf, where $D$ is the space dual. It is a group isomorphism: apply [lem-sc-rigidity] to
$$h(s,t)=\psi^{-1}(\psi(s+t)-\psi(s)-\psi(t)):C^\vee\times C^\vee\to C^\vee.$$
The first factor is proper geometrically connected and geometrically reduced by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]; the second is connected and the target separated of finite type. Since $h(s,0)=0$, rigidity makes $h$ independent of $s$, and $h(0,t)=0$ makes it zero. Thus the biadditivity and dual-pullback isomorphisms in the space node hold for exactly the dual and Poincare sheaf in this item. Uniqueness of representation identifies its $\phi_L$ and $a^\vee$ with those of the item as well.

source.place: I §§8–9, pp.36–41; comparison of representing duals and group laws written out

proof.text:
Write $P(z,b)$ for the fibre of the normalized Poincare sheaf. Use the two axis-preserving tensor laws of [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus]. They are associative, symmetric within either addition law, and satisfy interchange between the laws. Indeed, each of the two composites in any such diagram is an isomorphism between the same line modules, and preserves the rigidification at the first identity. Their quotient is a rigidification-preserving automorphism on $C\times T$, with the other coordinates included in $T$, hence is the identity by the automorphism clause of that node. This also proves compatibility with an axis-preserving pullback comparison. Iterating the laws therefore gives unambiguous maps
$$P(z,b)^{\otimes m}\simeq P(mz,b),\qquad P(z,b)^{\otimes m}\simeq P(z,mb).$$
Tensor pullback and its action on pure tensors are [lem-weil-pbc-module-pullback-tensor]. All later comparisons use these normalized maps, not arbitrary trivializations of point fibres.

source.place: I §§8–9, normalized universal family; coherence supplied by the uniqueness clause of the cited relative Poincare node

proof.text:
For $m=\ell^n$, $x\in A[m](k)$ and $b\in A^\vee[m](k)$, the two maps of step 2, followed by the identity-axis trivializations, give
$$t^1_m(x,b),t^2_m(x,b):P(x,b)^{\otimes m}\longrightarrow k.$$
Define $r_m(x,b)\in k^\times$ by $t^1_m=r_m t^2_m$. This is independent of any choice of a basis in $P(x,b)$. To check additivity in $x$, use $P(x+x',b)\simeq P(x,b)\otimes P(x',b)$. Interchange identifies each $t^i_m(x+x',b)$ with $t^i_m(x,b)\otimes t^i_m(x',b)$, so taking ratios gives $r_m(x+x',b)=r_m(x,b)r_m(x',b)$. The second tensor law gives the same equality in $b$. The axis maps give $r_m(0,b)=r_m(x,0)=1$, hence $r_m(x,b)^m=r_m(mx,b)=1$. Thus $r_m$ has values in $\mu_m(k)$. This two-trivialization construction is the finite Poincare Weil pairing, with the ratio convention $t^1/t^2$; set $w_{A,n}=r_{\ell^n}$.

source.place: I §13, p.57, finite pairing; Poincare-fibre construction of the same pairing expanded from §§8–9

proof.text:
For nondegeneracy, fix $b\in A^\vee[m](k)$ and let $M=P(-,b)$. For arbitrary $z\in A$, the first tensor law identifies $[m]^*M$ at $z$ with $P(z,b)^{\otimes m}$; the second law and $mb=0$ give a trivialization $\sigma:[m]^*M\simeq\mathcal O_A$. The map $q=[m]:A\to A$ is finite flat and surjective by [lem-sc-mult-n-finite-flat] and [lem-sc-mult-n-isogeny], hence is an fpqc covering. Its kernel $H=A[m]$ is finite etale by [lem-sc-ntorsion-etale]. Over the algebraically closed field $k$, [lem-exc-etale-field-gsets] identifies $H$ with the constant scheme on $H(k)$ (the absolute Galois group is trivial). The group-law formulas give the isomorphism
$$A\times H\simeq A\times_{q,A,q}A,\quad (z,x)\mapsto(z,z+x),$$
whose inverse subtracts the first coordinate from the second. Consequently a trivialization of $q^*M$ is a morphism of descent data precisely when it is invariant under these translations, for every $x\in H(k)$.

source.place: I §9, pp.41–42, kernel/character description of duality; I §13 p.57; fpqc cover and its overlap written explicitly

proof.text: Under the first-addition identification $P(z+x,b)\simeq P(z,b)\otimes P(x,b)$, the second-law trivialization $\sigma$ gains the factor $t^2_m(x,b)$. The canonical deck identification of $q^*M$ gains $t^1_m(x,b)$ instead: its base points agree since $m(z+x)=mz$. Their quotient is $t^2_m/t^1_m=r_m(x,b)^{-1}$. Interchange in [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus] justifies these identifications on the whole overlap, not just its individual fibres. If $r_m(x,b)=1$ for all $x$, $\sigma$ is therefore a compatible trivialization of the canonical descent datum. Apply the compatible-trivialization clause of [lem-pc-fpqc-descent], with the fpqc singleton $q$ of step 4, to conclude $M\simeq\mathcal O_A$. Rescale this isomorphism by its nonzero value at $0$ so that it respects the rigidification. The representing property in [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus] then implies $b=0$. This proves injectivity of $A^\vee[m](k)\to\operatorname{Hom}(A[m](k),\mu_m(k))$.

source.place: I §9, pp.41–42, descent-character proof; Stacks Tag 023T, descent-proposition-fpqc-descent-quasi-coherent

proof.text: Put $g=\dim A=\dim A^\vee$, the equality being part of [lem-sfb-abelian-polarization-calculus]. By [lem-sc-ntorsion-etale], both torsion groups are isomorphic to $(\mathbf Z/m\mathbf Z)^{2g}$. By [lem-sc-primitive-root], $\mu_m(k)$ is cyclic of order $m$. Every character of $(\mathbf Z/m\mathbf Z)^{2g}$ is uniquely determined by the $2g$ arbitrary images of its coordinate generators. Thus its character group has $m^{2g}$ elements. The injection of step 5 is consequently a bijection. These characters separate points: for a nonzero coordinate $c\bmod m$, the character sending its generator to a primitive $m$-th root $\zeta$ takes the value $\zeta^c\ne1$. Surjectivity from step 5 therefore implies injectivity of the other evaluation map. Its source and target again have $m^{2g}$ elements, so it too is bijective. This proves both asserted perfectness clauses, including $g=0$.

source.place: I §13 p.57, nondegeneracy; I §9 p.41, Cartier-dual description; elementary finite-coordinate count

proof.text: Let $M=mr$, $u\in A[M](k)$ and $v\in A^\vee[M](k)$. The two tensor laws identify $P(ru,rv)^{\otimes m}$ with $P(u,v)^{\otimes mr^2}$. Expand $t^1_m(ru,rv)$ by first adding $r$ copies of $u$, then $m$ copies, and expand the second variable into $r$ copies of $v$. Associativity and interchange from step 2 identify the result with $(t^1_M(u,v))^{\otimes r}$. Expanding in the opposite order gives $t^2_m(ru,rv)=(t^2_M(u,v))^{\otimes r}$ under the same identification. Taking ratios yields $r_m(ru,rv)=r_M(u,v)^r$. With $m=\ell^n$ and $r=\ell$, this is precisely $w_{A,n}(\ell u,\ell v)=w_{A,n+1}(u,v)^\ell$. In particular the exponent is $\ell$, despite multiplication by $\ell$ in both input coordinates.

source.place: I Lemma 13.1, p.57; expansion of the two normalized tensor-power maps

proof.text: For $a:A\to B$, use the axis-preserving comparison $(a\times1)^*P_B\simeq(1\times a^\vee)^*P_A$ of [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus], identified in step 1 with the dual pullback fixed in the statement. It identifies $P_B(ax,y)$ with $P_A(x,a^\vee y)$. Here $a$ is a homomorphism by hypothesis, and $a^\vee$ is one as well: pulling back the trivial rigidified family gives $a^\vee(0)=0$, so the morphism $h(s,t)=a^\vee(s+t)-a^\vee(s)-a^\vee(t):B^\vee\times B^\vee\to A^\vee$ satisfies $h(s,0)=0$ and $h(0,t)=0$, and [lem-sc-rigidity] applies exactly as in step 1 (the first factor is proper, geometrically connected and geometrically reduced by [lem-sc-abelian-variety-characterization]), giving $h=0$. Because $a$ and $a^\vee$ are group homomorphisms, it carries the first $m$-fold addition map to the first and the second to the second; these are the normalized comparisons whose uniqueness was checked in step 2. It also carries each axis trivialization to the corresponding one. Therefore it identifies $t^1_m$ on the two fibres and separately identifies $t^2_m$. Their ratios give $r_{B,m}(ax,y)=r_{A,m}(x,a^\vee y)$, the claimed finite adjunction identity.

source.place: I §9 opening paragraph p.41; finite version of Proposition 13.2(a), p.58, proved directly on the Poincare sheaf

proof.text:
For an arbitrary invertible $L$, pull the Poincare sheaf back by $1\times\phi_L$. By [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus] and step 1 this is
$$N_L=m_A^*L\otimes p_1^*L^{-1}\otimes p_2^*L^{-1}\otimes q^*0^*L.$$
Commutativity of $A$ [lem-sc-av-commutative] makes this normalized family symmetric under swapping $x,y$: the $m_A^*L$ and constant factors are unchanged, and the other two factors are interchanged by the ordinary tensor symmetry. This isomorphism preserves both axis trivializations. Consequently it swaps the first and second tensor-addition laws: each resulting comparison preserves the first identity rigidification, so uniqueness in [lem-sfb-abelian-space-poincare-calculus] makes the two composites equal. On $m$-torsion fibres it thus carries $t^1_m(x,\phi_Ly)$ to $t^2_m(y,\phi_Lx)$ and $t^2_m(x,\phi_Ly)$ to $t^1_m(y,\phi_Lx)$. Taking ratios proves
$$r_m(x,\phi_Ly)=r_m(y,\phi_Lx)^{-1}.$$
This argument uses the normalized difference family for every invertible $L$, without an isogeny or ampleness hypothesis. It proves skew symmetry also for $\ell=2$, without dividing by $2$.
